## The Old Archbishop's Palace in Mexico City: architecture, museum and ancient temple

**Antiguo Palacio del Arzobispado**, the Old Archbishop's Palace, stands on Moneda Street in the historic centre of [Mexico City](/mexico/place/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/), near [Zócalo Square](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/). Today, the building houses the **Art Museum of Mexico's Ministry of Finance and Public Credit (Museo de Arte de la SHCP)**. There are three reasons to explore it: its historic facade, collections of Mexican art and traces of structures that predate the colonial city.

Unlike the [National Palace](/mexico/place/national-palace-mexico-city/), which houses government institutions and Diego Rivera's famous murals, the former archbishops' residence is a separate museum site. You can conveniently visit both on the same walk, but their addresses and visiting rules should not be confused.

## Where is the building and how can you recognise it?

The museum is at **Moneda 4**, near the intersection with Licenciado Primo Verdad Street. These blocks lie east of the Zócalo, close to [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/) and other historic-centre monuments.

The palace has a distinctive stone facade with balconies and a richly decorated entrance portal. Arcades and galleries surround its inner courtyards. Look closely at the stonework, columns and ornamental features characteristic of colonial Mexico City.

A visit complements the [Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/) and historic buildings around the Zócalo. This compact neighbourhood contains everything from ecclesiastical institutions to civic architecture.

## How the palace is connected to New Spain's first archbishop

In the 16th century, Bishop Juan de Zumárraga chose this site for his residence. The building was later rebuilt and expanded repeatedly. The main features of the large palace complex date from the colonial era; the current courtyards and facade reflect changes accumulated over several centuries.

The history of the building intertwines the religious and administrative life of New Spain. This helps explain why the residence stood so close to the colonial capital's main squares, churches and institutions.

Yet the history of the site goes back much further.

## What is known about the temple of Tezcatlipoca beneath the palace?

Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) reports **ancient structures associated with the worship of Tezcatlipoca** discovered beneath the building and within its foundations. The museum complex includes archaeological viewing windows displaying sections of pre-Hispanic structures.

This is particularly interesting after a visit to [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/): there you can see the principal ceremonial complex of Tenochtitlan, while here evidence of the ancient city is preserved inside a colonial building. Some archaeological areas have restricted access, however; their inclusion in the museum's collections **does not mean that every viewing window is open to the public**.

## What art is displayed at the SHCP museum?

The museum is known for its **Pago en Especie** and **Acervo Patrimonial** collections. The former relates to a Mexican system allowing artists to settle tax obligations by transferring works of art. The latter brings together historic and artistic objects collected and preserved by the government department.

Exhibitions may include paintings, graphic works, sculpture and decorative arts. Displays change, so check the museum's current programme for specific paintings, artists and galleries. The collections provide an opportunity to experience Mexican art beyond the capital's best-known tourist museums.

| Your interest | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Architecture | Entrance portal, arcades and courtyards |
| Church history | The archbishops' residence |
| Archaeology | Remains of the temple of Tezcatlipoca |
| Art | SHCP collections and exhibitions |

## Including the palace in a walk through Mexico City

A historic-centre walk can combine the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), [Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/), [National Palace](/mexico/place/national-palace-mexico-city/), [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/) and the museum at 4 Moneda Street. Public squares and exterior facades have different access conditions from museums and government buildings, so adjust the order of visits to the actual entry arrangements.

On our [7-day religious journey through Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), the Old Archbishop's Palace is one of the stops on the third day in Mexico City. That day also features churches in the historic centre and an evening visit to [Garibaldi Square](/mexico/place/garibaldi-plaza/). Listing a museum as a stop does not promise entry to every gallery: the specific visit is governed by the itinerary.

## Frequently asked questions about the Old Archbishop's Palace

### Where is the Old Archbishop's Palace in Mexico City?

At Moneda 4, close to the historic centre and the Zócalo. The building now houses the Mexican Ministry of Finance's art museum.

### Is it the same National Palace that contains Rivera's murals?

No. The [National Palace](/mexico/place/national-palace-mexico-city/) is a separate government complex by the Zócalo. The former archbishops' residence is on Moneda Street and has its own museum collections.

### Can I see remains of a pre-Hispanic temple?

Archaeological investigations identified elements of the temple of Tezcatlipoca here, some displayed through special museum viewing windows. Check whether the relevant area is open before travelling.

### Do I need a separate museum ticket?

Official cultural directories and INAH describe free admission to certain museum and archaeological exhibitions. Nevertheless, confirm opening times, current exhibitions and entrance arrangements immediately before visiting.

## Tours visiting the Old Archbishop's Palace in Mexico City

The [Old Archbishop's Palace](/mexico/place/old-archbishop-palace/) stands on Moneda Street in central [Mexico City](/mexico/), near the Zócalo. Behind its facade are layers of history: ancient Tenochtitlan, the early Catholic Church in New Spain and a present-day art museum.

We offer {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} including a visit to the palace. Our [Religious Journey through Mexico: 7 Days](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) is scheduled for **April 1–7, 2027**; the palace is included on **day 3, April 3**. This is not a dedicated museum tour: the palace is part of a wider pilgrimage sightseeing excursion focusing on religious architecture, the capital's history and churches.

### Why this combination works

One walking route connects the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), [Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/), [Santo Domingo Church](/mexico/place/santo-domingo-mexico-city/) and the former archbishops' residence. This sequence makes sense: from the public square and great cathedral to a smaller church and then the building of the ecclesiastical administration.

Towards the end of the day, the itinerary introduces another facet of city life: [Garibaldi Square](/mexico/place/garibaldi-plaza/) and its mariachi musicians. It represents secular urban culture, while the daytime route concentrates on religious history.

## What's included in the April 3 excursion?

In the morning, the group heads into the capital's historic centre. Following the Zócalo, **Holy Mass is scheduled at Santo Domingo Church**, followed by visits to the Metropolitan Cathedral, National Palace and Old Archbishop's Palace. Travellers then continue to Garibaldi Square. The separate [Mexico City Churches, Mass and Garibaldi Square excursion](/mexico/santo-domingo-mexico-city/mexico-city-pilgrimage-garibaldi/) describes these stops as one programme.

| Site | Its role in the day |
|---|---|
| Zócalo | Historic centre |
| Santo Domingo | Holy Mass |
| Metropolitan Cathedral | The capital's principal cathedral |
| Archbishop's Palace | History and art |
| Garibaldi | Mariachi tradition |

Distinguish **visiting the palace itself** from accessing all of its museum galleries. The itinerary names the palace as a stop but does not guarantee a particular temporary exhibition or a specific number of open rooms. A similar restriction applies to the [National Palace](/mexico/place/national-palace-mexico-city/): as a government building, it may close to visitors during official events.

After the excursion, the group returns to the hotel for dinner. There is no overnight stay in another city.

## From Juan de Zumárraga's residence to an art museum

In the early colonial period, this area became the residence of Mexico's first bishop, **Juan de Zumárraga**. The building was rebuilt many times afterwards. It is now known as the **Museo de Arte de la Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público**, the Mexican Ministry of Finance's art museum. Its changing functions reflect the historic centre, where religious buildings stand alongside government and cultural institutions.

Before the palace was built, this site held a temple dedicated to **Tezcatlipoca**, an important deity in Aztec religion. Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History documents archaeological remains of the structure, displayed through special viewing windows. The building's history thus predates Spanish colonisation by a long time.

Look at the stone portal, courtyards and passages between galleries. The meeting of historic architecture and a modern museum makes this stop interesting even if religion is not the purpose of your trip. The name "Archbishop's Palace" describes its **historic function**, not a present-day residence of a church leader.

### What is the museum like?

Its galleries display works from the Ministry of Finance collections, including artworks transferred to the state through a tax-payment-in-kind scheme. Particular exhibitions change. Official museum and archaeological sources also describe the "archaeological windows" showing remains of Tezcatlipoca's temple, but the presence of these exhibits in the institution **does not guarantee** that they are all part of the Ada Tours excursion.

The museum stands on Moneda Street close to other attractions in the old centre. If visiting independently, check both museum opening hours and access to the archaeological areas: these may have different entry arrangements, and a future itinerary cannot replace the museum's current timetable.

## The palace's place in the pilgrimage itinerary

The seven-day trip includes **5 Holy Masses** and several contrasting cities. In Mexico City the group visits the [Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/) and the anthropology museum. After the day featuring the Archbishop's Palace, travellers visit [Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/), [Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/) and [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/), followed by [Cuernavaca](/mexico/place/cuernavaca/) and [Taxco](/mexico/place/taxco/).

The itinerary distinguishes liturgical stops from educational ones. Mass on April 3 takes place at Santo Domingo. The palace helps visitors understand colonial church administration and changes to urban buildings after Mexican independence. Garibaldi Square later that day provides a chance to experience a living musical tradition.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_mexico_religious_journey}}

## Practical travel arrangements

The group spends all **6 nights** in Mexico City in a standard room at **Casa Blanca 4\*** or a hotel of similar category. The programme includes private transfers and excursions with an English-speaking guide, breakfasts and dinners according to the itinerary, entry tickets to the listed sites and 5 Masses. International flights, drinks and personal expenses are paid separately.

**No fixed tour price has been published.** When comparing options, consider the overall package, guiding language, liturgical programme and exact dates rather than simply the visit to the palace.

Comfortable walking shoes are useful in the historic centre. The itinerary includes churches, museums and busy pedestrian streets. Choose clothing appropriate for church services and follow the current rules on photography and filming inside museums.

## Frequently asked questions

### On which day is the Old Archbishop's Palace scheduled?

On **April 3, 2027**, the third day of the trip. Before that, the group visits Guadalupe and the anthropology museum; afterwards it explores sacred sites in Tlaxcala and Puebla.

### Where is Mass celebrated during this excursion?

At **Santo Domingo Church**. The Old Archbishop's Palace is a cultural and historical stop, not the site of the scheduled Mass.

### Is the palace still used as an archbishop's residence?

No, the name is historic. The building now houses the Mexican Ministry of Finance's art museum.

### Can viewing the archaeological remains of Tezcatlipoca's temple be guaranteed?

Official sources confirm that the building contains dedicated archaeological displays. However, the published itinerary does not promise access to **every** such room. Entry depends on the museum's operations and the excursion schedule.

### Why might history enthusiasts enjoy this journey as well as pilgrims?

The pilgrimage connects [Mexico City churches](/mexico/santo-domingo-mexico-city/mexico-city-pilgrimage-garibaldi/), colonial cities, [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) and religious monuments. Our [7-day itinerary page](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) explains the combination in greater detail.

## The Palace of Cortés in Cuernavaca: what lies behind the fortress walls?

One of the oldest surviving civic buildings in colonial [Mexico](/mexico/) stands in the historic centre of [Cuernavaca](/mexico/place/cuernavaca/). Known as the Palace of Cortés, its massive stone walls, arcades and corner sections resemble a fortified residence. For visitors, it is both a 16th-century landmark and a museum telling the history of the peoples of what is now Morelos state.

The building is associated with Hernán Cortés, but its museum narrative begins long before the Spanish conquest. It is therefore particularly rewarding for travellers who want to understand how the city and surrounding region changed, not merely see conquistador architecture.

## From pre-Hispanic Cuernavaca to the marquis's residence

Cortés ordered the construction of a residence and administrative centre for his estate, the Marquisate of the Valley of Oaxaca. According to Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), the main phase of construction was completed by 1535. The palace shows the practical architecture of the early colonial period: stone walls, austere openings and interior rooms designed for different purposes.

Archaeological investigations have revealed several phases of earlier construction beneath the building associated with the Tlahuica people. This is an essential part of the site's history: the Spanish residence was built on land already inhabited and developed. In the museum, consider how these archaeological layers relate to later buildings rather than treating the 16th century as the beginning of Cuernavaca's story.

## What is inside the Museum of the Peoples of Morelos?

The former palace houses the **Regional Museum of the Peoples of Morelos** (*Museo Regional de los Pueblos de Morelos*). Its collections explore pre-Hispanic cultures, the colonial period and subsequent events. Archaeological objects are placed in the context of changing land use, society and the region's political history.

Mexican independence, 19th-century reforms and the Mexican Revolution have particular prominence. These subjects are especially important to Morelos because of the region's connection with Emiliano Zapata's movement. Allow time for maps, interpretation and historic objects: they help explain why a relatively small state has an important place in the country's history.

### Diego Rivera's murals

In the palace's upper gallery is a monumental mural by **Diego Rivera** depicting the history of Morelos. The artist worked on it from 1927 to 1930 at the request of American ambassador Dwight Morrow. The composition includes scenes of conquest, historical figures and events important to the region's people.

The mural is both a work of art and a 20th-century interpretation of history. Compare its story with the museum galleries: the exhibition and the artist may emphasise different aspects of the same events. The gallery's arches also become part of the composition, showing how the painting interacts with the building's architecture.

## Planning a visit to the palace

The museum is in the city centre near Jardín Juárez. A good plan is to view the building from outside, visit the exhibition, then return to the square, giving you a clearer sense of the different periods. Allow dedicated time to explore the museum rather than treating it as a brief facade photo stop.

Check opening hours, ticket prices, access to particular galleries and current restrictions with INAH before travelling, as arrangements can change. Extra rules may apply to photography and larger groups.

After the museum, continue to [Cuernavaca Cathedral](/mexico/place/cuernavaca-cathedral/). The palace presents civic power and the history of Morelos's people, while the cathedral complex illustrates early religious architecture. Together they offer a fuller view of the city. For wider regional travel, see the [cultural and historical tours in Mexico](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/mexico/).

## Frequently asked questions about the Palace of Cortés

### Is the Palace of Cortés still an occupied residence?

No. The historic building now contains a regional museum dedicated to the peoples and history of Morelos.

### Is the museum only about Hernán Cortés?

No. Its themes span the pre-Hispanic past, colonial period and later centuries, including the Mexican Revolution.

### Can I see Diego Rivera's work here?

Yes. The building preserves Rivera's monumental mural about the history of Morelos. Check which museum areas are accessible before visiting.

### What can I combine with the palace in Cuernavaca?

Visit [Cuernavaca Cathedral](/mexico/place/cuernavaca-cathedral/) and walk through the [city's historic centre](/mexico/place/cuernavaca/). These stops allow you to compare 16th-century civic and monastic architecture.

## Which tours visit the Palace of Cortés?

The [Palace of Cortés](/mexico/place/palace-of-cortes/) stands in central [Cuernavaca](/mexico/place/cuernavaca/), the capital of Mexico's Morelos state. Its massive stone walls retain the character of an early colonial residence, while the museum exhibitions tell the region's broader history, from indigenous peoples to modern culture.

We offer {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that visit the palace on their main itinerary. The confirmed departure is the [Religious Journey through Mexico: 7 Days](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), scheduled for **April 1–7, 2027**. The palace is visited on **day 5, April 5**, together with Cuernavaca Cathedral and the town of Taxco.

The order matters: the morning is devoted to Cuernavaca's architecture and history, before the route continues to a Baroque church in Taxco. There is no overnight stay in either Cuernavaca or Taxco; the group returns to Mexico City in the evening.

## April 5: Cuernavaca and Taxco

After breakfast, travellers leave Mexico City by private transport with an English-speaking guide. In Cuernavaca they visit the [Palace of Cortés](/mexico/place/palace-of-cortes/) and [Cathedral](/mexico/place/cuernavaca-cathedral/). The journey continues to [Taxco](/mexico/place/taxco/), known for silversmithing and streets climbing the hillsides. **Holy Mass at Santa Prisca Church** is scheduled there.

| Stop | What's included |
|---|---|
| Palace of Cortés | Historic building |
| Cuernavaca Cathedral | Cathedral complex |
| Taxco | Walking tour of the town |
| Santa Prisca | Holy Mass |

The day is described in more detail in the separate [Cuernavaca, Taxco and Mass at Santa Prisca excursion](/mexico/cuernavaca/cuernavaca-taxco-pilgrimage/). Private transportation, an English-speaking guide, admission tickets to the listed attractions and one Mass are included in that excursion.

**Mass takes place in Taxco**, not at the Palace of Cortés or Cuernavaca Cathedral. This distinction is particularly important on a pilgrimage: the historical and liturgical stops in one day serve different purposes.

## What makes the Palace of Cortés significant?

The building is associated with **Hernán Cortés** and the first decades of the Spanish conquest of central Mexico. Its main construction phase ended in the 16th century, around **1535**. The site also has an earlier history: structures built by the Tlahuica people stood here before the colonial residence. Its story therefore goes well beyond the biography of a single conquistador.

The palace's architecture differs noticeably from the ornate facades of Baroque churches visited on other days. Thick stone walls and a fortified appearance recall how residence, administration and displays of authority were combined in early New Spain.

Today the building houses the **Regional Museum of the Peoples of Morelos** (Museo Regional de los Pueblos de Morelos). Following restoration, the museum reopened under this name in 2023. Its exhibitions cover archaeology, nature, cultural diversity and the history of Morelos state, revealing both its colonial era and earlier and more recent life.

### What to look for during the visit

Begin with the building itself: interior spaces, passageways, stonework and its setting in the historic centre. If museum galleries are open on the excursion date, you may then explore exhibitions on the peoples of Morelos.

**The palace visit is part of the route**, but the itinerary does not specify particular galleries or temporary exhibitions. The museum decides which are open, and access hours can change. This matters especially for a visit scheduled on a particular day in 2027.

The museum is in central Cuernavaca. Independent travellers should check the conditions for visiting the museum itself, rather than merely whether the square outside is open.

## How the palace differs from the itinerary's other stops

[Cuernavaca Cathedral](/mexico/place/cuernavaca-cathedral/) forms part of a Franciscan monastic complex. It illustrates the establishment of Catholic institutions in the region and the architecture of the church. The Palace of Cortés represents civic and administrative construction from the same broad historical period.

In [Taxco](/mexico/place/taxco/), the journey moves to a later era: [Santa Prisca Church](/mexico/place/santa-prisca-taxco/) is famous for Baroque decoration and tall towers rising among the white houses of the mountain town. This is where participants attend Mass.

The combination suits travellers interested in **Mexican history, architecture and religious culture**. The palace reveals civic history, the cathedral reflects the missionary period, and Santa Prisca represents later Baroque architecture.

## How the palace fits into the 7-day tour

The journey begins in Mexico City. Before Cuernavaca, the group visits the [Shrine of Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/), churches in the historic centre and the [Old Archbishop's Palace](/mexico/place/old-archbishop-palace/), then travels to [Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/), [Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/) and [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/). After Cuernavaca, the itinerary continues via [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco.

**All 6 nights are spent in Mexico City**, so the April 4 and 5 excursions are day trips without changing hotels. Five Holy Masses are scheduled on different days. Transfers, overnight arrangements and excursion order are important: a visit to Cuernavaca should not be assumed to provide a free day for exploring all of the city's museums independently.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_mexico_religious_journey}}

## Format, accommodation and things to check

Our tour includes a standard room at **Casa Blanca 4\*** or a hotel of comparable category for 6 nights, private transfers and excursions, an English-speaking guide, breakfasts and dinners according to the itinerary, entrance tickets and arrangements for 5 Masses. For groups of up to 24 people, a minibus is provided; from 25 participants, a touring coach is used. Flights, drinks and personal spending are excluded.

**The itinerary page does not give a fixed tour price.** Comparing this package with a one-day Cuernavaca trip solely by the number of sites visited would be misleading: the full package price also covers accommodation, transport and additional excursion days.

Consider what matters to you. If the Morelos museum exhibitions are a priority, remember that time in Cuernavaca is limited by the onward journey to Taxco. If your main goal is pilgrimage, the day's key event takes place later, at Santa Prisca Church. Comfortable shoes are advisable for historic streets and several consecutive stops.

## Frequently asked questions

### On which day does the tour visit the Palace of Cortés?

On **April 5, 2027**, day five of the 7-day Mexico journey. After Cuernavaca, the group visits Taxco and returns to Mexico City.

### Is the Palace of Cortés an operating museum?

Yes. It houses the **Regional Museum of the Peoples of Morelos**, which reopened after restoration in 2023. Visiting particular galleries during the tour nevertheless depends on time and exhibition access.

### Is Mass celebrated in Cuernavaca?

On the confirmed itinerary, that day's Mass takes place **at Santa Prisca Church in Taxco**. The Palace of Cortés and Cuernavaca Cathedral are listed as sightseeing stops.

### Do travellers stay overnight in Cuernavaca?

No. All 6 nights are in Mexico City; the group returns to the capital after visiting Cuernavaca and Taxco.

### Is this journey worth choosing for the history of colonial Mexico?

Yes. It includes the [Old Archbishop's Palace in Mexico City](/mexico/place/old-archbishop-palace/), the [Palace of Cortés](/mexico/place/palace-of-cortes/), the monastery complexes of Tlaxcala and Puebla's churches. For the duration, guided services and remaining days, see the [full journey itinerary](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/).

## Palenque in Mexico: an ancient Maya city amid the jungle

**Palenque is an archaeological site in Chiapas state in southeastern [Mexico](/mexico/).** A modern town has the same name, so distinguish between the town where you stay and the archaeological zone when planning. The principal ancient structures stand amid dense forest at the foot of the mountains.

Palenque belongs to the Classic period of Maya civilisation. Temples, palace rooms, reliefs and inscriptions survive, allowing researchers to reconstruct the rulers' history. In 1987, the monument and the surrounding natural area received UNESCO World Heritage status.

## The Temple of the Inscriptions and the ruler Pakal

**The Temple of the Inscriptions (Templo de las Inscripciones)** is one of the city's most famous monuments. In the 20th century, archaeologists discovered the tomb of K'inich Janaab' Pakal inside it. The discovery helped explain the political and religious life of the Maya kingdom.

The temple takes its name from lengthy hieroglyphic inscriptions containing information about the dynasty. A guide's explanation of how the Maya recorded dates and events brings the stone structures to life as part of the story of real people.

Access to certain interior rooms and burial areas may be restricted. Admission to the archaeological zone does not guarantee entry into the tomb itself. Current rules are determined by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH).

## What else is there to see in the archaeological zone?

**The Palace** is a large building complex with courtyards and a tower. It helps visitors imagine the administrative and ceremonial life of the ancient city. Squares, platforms and other temples stand nearby.

Another highlight is **the Group of the Cross**, comprising the Temple of the Cross, Temple of the Sun and Temple of the Foliated Cross. Their inscriptions and reliefs relate to rituals and dynastic history. Moving between these parts of the archaeological site involves paths and stone steps.

| Site | Main interest |
|---|---|
| Temple of the Inscriptions | The ruler Pakal |
| Palace | Architecture and royal power |
| Group of the Cross | Religious reliefs |
| Site museum | Finds and history |

If your visit is short, spend time at the principal complexes rather than attempting to cover every trace of ancient construction. The archaeological area extends far beyond the section open to tourists.

## What distinguishes Palenque from other Maya cities?

At [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/), visitors see monumental buildings of the Yucatán against a relatively open landscape. Palenque is much more humid and green: the forest reaches the temples and mountain slopes change the impression of the architecture.

Palenque is especially rewarding for anyone interested in the history of rulers and in reading monuments as historical evidence. Besides pyramids, its inscriptions, sculptures and palace layout are important. These sites complement one another on a journey through Maya culture, although travelling between the Yucatán and Chiapas requires long transfers or separate transport arrangements.

Palenque's historical importance does not depend on the size of a single pyramid. The city is distinguished by its combination of architecture, art and written records.

## Waterfalls and nature near Palenque

The surrounding Chiapas region offers natural stops to complement an archaeological excursion. Tourist itineraries feature **Misol-Ha** and other waterfalls with forest paths. However, the waterfalls and the ruins are separate attractions: visiting one does not mean the other is automatically included.

The area has a warm, humid climate, making weather and path conditions important for waterfall outings. Stone surfaces can be slippery after rain. Swimming in natural pools is permitted only where local authorities allow it and conditions are safe.

Experiencing tropical nature alongside history can be rewarding, but sightings of specific animals should not be promised. Experienced guides and conservation rules matter on nature excursions.

## Getting there and how much time to allow

Modern Palenque is the starting point for visits to the ancient city. The archaeological area lies outside the town centre, so plan a transfer to the entrance and separate time for walking. INAH publishes visiting hours and ticketing arrangements, which can change; check the official information before travelling.

For a first visit, allow several hours and focus on the main complexes. If you also want to see the museum, enjoy a full guided tour and visit waterfalls, allow extra time or another full day.

Conditions near the ruins are hot and humid. Take water, shoes with good grip, a hat and insect protection. Despite the surrounding forest, sunlight can be strong in exposed areas.

## Frequently asked questions about Palenque

### Is Palenque a town or an archaeological site?

Both a modern town and an ancient Maya site bear that name. Visiting the ruins requires a separate trip from the town.

### What is the Temple of the Inscriptions famous for?

It contains the burial complex of the ruler Pakal, and its hieroglyphic inscriptions help researchers study the history of the Maya kingdom.

### Can I explore Palenque in one day?

Yes. The principal monuments can be visited on a day excursion. The museum, longer walks and waterfalls require more time.

### Is Pakal's tomb open to tourists?

INAH regulates access to the interior. Having the temple on an itinerary does not guarantee entry to its burial chamber.
